# Project Links do not work on Wamp Server

When configuring a local development environment on Windows using Wamp Server, it is common to encounter redirect loops where relative URLs resolve incorrectly. Specifically, hovering over links in your `www` directory reveals that they resolve to `http://ProjectFolderNameHere/` instead of the expected `http://localhost:8080/ProjectFolderNameHere/`. This behavior indicates a fundamental misconfiguration in how the web server handles hostnames and port redirections, rather than a simple CSS or JavaScript issue.

The root cause lies in the default virtual host configuration within the Apache module of Wamp Server. By default, when you install Apache via Wamp on Windows, it is often configured to redirect all traffic from `localhost` to a specific port (like 8080) if port 80 is occupied or misconfigured, but critically, it may not be explicitly binding the virtual host to `localhost:8080`. Instead, Apache might be listening on `localhost` with a generic document root configuration that causes it to treat requests as if they are coming from the folder name itself when no specific host header matches.

To resolve this, you must inspect the default virtual host file, typically located at `apache\conf\extra\httpd-vhosts.conf`. In many Wamp Server setups, you will find a configuration block that looks like this:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    DocumentRoot "C:/wamp/www/ProjectFolderNameHere"
    ServerName localhost
</VirtualHost>
```

If your Wamp installation is configured to use port 8080 globally, the virtual host directive must explicitly specify that port. If the configuration relies on a rewrite rule to redirect `localhost` to `localhost:8080`, ensure that the `ServerName` directive matches the hostname you are actually accessing.

However, the specific symptom describedâwhere links resolve to the project folder name without the domain prefixâsuggests that Apache is not receiving or processing the `Host` header correctly for port 8080 requests. This often happens if the default virtual host on port 80 is active and redirecting traffic in a way that strips the path or hostname before the application receives it.

The most robust fix involves ensuring your Wamp configuration explicitly defines a VirtualHost for port 8080. Update your `httpd-vhosts.conf` to include:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:8080>
    DocumentRoot "C:/wamp/www/ProjectFolderNameHere"
    ServerName localhost
    ServerAlias www.localhost
</VirtualHost>
```

After making these changes, you must restart the Apache service within the Wamp control panel to apply the new configuration without reloading IIS. Since you mentioned disabling Microsoft IIS, ensure that no residual services are conflicting with the Wamp stack. On Windows 7, sometimes the `localhost` entry in the hosts file or lingering DNS cache can cause confusion, but given your setup, the Apache virtual host definition is the primary suspect.

It is also worth noting that if you are using a framework like Laravel or Symfony, ensure that your `.env` file and application configuration explicitly set the `APP_URL` to `http://localhost:8080`. If the server sends a 301 redirect incorrectly due to a mismatch between the incoming `Host` header and the configured `ServerName`, the application might generate absolute links based on the redirected URL, leading to the observed behavior.

By explicitly binding the VirtualHost to port 8080 and ensuring the `DocumentRoot` points to your actual project directory, you guarantee that every request to `http://localhost:8080/ProjectFolderNameHere` is served with the correct context. This prevents the browser from interpreting the path as a subdomain or a relative path without a base URL.

For further guidance on configuring local development environments and ensuring your application routes are correctly resolved, you may refer to resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com), which often provides detailed troubleshooting for common Wamp Server issues encountered by developers working with PHP frameworks.
